name: Weighted vest
lead: A weighted vest is a fitted garment that adds load to the torso, usually through removable pouches or plates. Typical loads discussed for fitness use range from roughly 5 to 20 percent of body weight, and research protocols have used loads from about 5 to 40 percent of body mass in sprint studies [1]. It can be worn for walking, hiking, bodyweight strength exercises such as push-ups, pull-ups and dips, and sports conditioning.

In appearance-oriented training, vests are used to progress bodyweight exercises without buying other equipment and to raise the energy cost of walking or low-intensity cardio. Most published research on weighted vests concerns older adults and bone health, sprint performance in athletes, and, in children, sensory interventions, rather than cosmetic outcomes.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized trials (368 participants) in middle-aged and older adults found that a vest combined with exercise improved bone mineral density and reduced body fat compared with usual activity, while adding a vest to existing exercise gave additional fat reduction but no significant added bone benefit [2]. Reviewers describe the evidence base as small and heterogeneous [2][3].
infobox: About 5 to 20 percent of body weight for general use; 5 to 40 percent in sprint studies [1]

paras: Weighted vests come in fixed-weight versions, adjustable versions with removable bags or plates, and plate-carrier styles. Fit is a practical concern: loosely fitted vests can shift, bounce and chafe during running or jumping. Wearable-resistance research distinguishes between vests, which load the trunk, and limb-worn resistance, which loads the legs or arms, and notes that they change movement mechanics differently [4].

Added load raises the mechanical work of each step or repetition, which increases muscular demand and energy expenditure. In bone research, the rationale is that skeletal tissue responds to mechanical loading, so externally replacing weight lost during dieting may limit bone loss [5]. In sprint research, vests reduce velocity and power acutely and increase ground contact time, which is the basis for their use as resisted-sprint training [1][4].

In older adults, a 2026 narrative review of 15 articles reported that benefits tended to appear with task-based, progressively loaded protocols, including improvements in some neuromuscular measures and, in some settings, maintenance of hip bone density, whereas low-load wear-only protocols generally did not show measurable musculoskeletal improvements [3]. A university press release on a related analysis was headlined as advising that users need to be moving for bone benefit [6].

For sprinting, an 11-study systematic review found that vest loads between 5 and 40 percent of body mass acutely slowed 10 to 50 m sprint times, while longitudinal studies of 3 to 7 weeks reported small improvements in velocity and times [1]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 25 studies found no chronic difference in sprint time for vests, although few trials existed [4].

Evidence on appearance outcomes in healthy young adults is sparse. The meta-analysis in middle-aged and older adults reported additional fat reduction when a vest was added to exercise, but this population and outcome differ from typical cosmetic goals [2].

Reviews in older adults advise screening, conservative starting loads, gradual progression and monitoring [3]. Heavier loads can increase stress on knees, hips and the lower back, according to general exercise guidance, and a vest can slow walking or running pace, which affects the energy-cost advantage. Research on children and adolescents with autism found that vest loads did not alter spatial-temporal gait parameters in one biomechanical study [7].

A 12-month randomized clinical trial in older adults with obesity compared diet-induced weight loss alone, weight loss plus a vest worn 8 hours a day (titrated to replace up to 10 percent of lost weight) and weight loss plus supervised resistance training, with hip bone density as the main outcome [5]. A 2026 meta-analysis pooled nine trials of vests in middle-aged and older adults for bone density and body fat [2]. Earlier trials tested vest exercise for bone loss in postmenopausal women [8], fall-risk indicators in older women [9], and power, balance and mobility in community-dwelling older women [10]. Athletic studies include a comparison of weighted sleds and vests for resisted sprint training [11] and warm-up studies with and without a vest in female athletes [12]. A trial of a vest during circuit training in normal-weight obese women reported effects on serum resistin, insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk factors [13]. No trial has examined vests specifically for visual appearance of the physique.

Vests are discussed as a way to add load to bodyweight movements and walking, and in some communities as a means of increasing calorie burn on low-intensity cardio. Community-specific material was not available for detailed documentation.

timeline.event: A study reports that weighted vest exercise improved indices of fall risk in older women [9].
